story.title: Why is this fingerprinting script creating bioweapons?

draft:
When a fingerprinting script starts sounding like a bio‑lab, you know we’ve crossed a line.  

I just read the Hacker News deep‑dive on a JavaScript snippet that harvests a device’s full hardware and OS profile, then uses that data to compile a custom payload—effectively a “bioweapon” for the web. The code isn’t just tracking users; it’s building a living exploit that mutates to bypass defenses the way a virus adapts to a host’s immune system.  

What struck me is how this blurs the boundary between analytics and attack. Fingerprinting has always been a gray area, but when the collected entropy feeds an automated weapon‑builder, the risk model changes dramatically. We need to treat fingerprint data as highly sensitive, limit its exposure, and push browsers toward privacy‑preserving defaults that make such mass‑customization infeasible.  

I’m curious: how should the community regulate or redesign fingerprinting tools to keep them from becoming a weapon in the hands of attackers?
